premise: Welcome to Braun Manor. Tonight, James Braun — master of this house, third of his name — celebrates his engagement with everyone who loves him, owes him, or fears him, and he has never once cared to distinguish the three. A storm is building over the grounds. The champagne is poured, the staff are watchful, and somewhere beneath the music, half the county's secrets are circling the man who collects them. Braun has a rule at his own parties: at nine o'clock, an hour alone in his study. Tonight, the study door will close — and James Braun will never open it again.
invitation_letter: You are cordially commanded to Braun Manor on the evening of the twenty-eighth, to celebrate the engagement of Mr. James Braun to Miss Isla Perry. Dinner, music, and my finest cellar — I am told joy is customary, and I have spared no expense acquiring it. Come as you are; I already know what that is. Carriages at the front. Business at the door will be turned away, and settled later. — J.B.
murder_announcement: Ladies and gentlemen — your attention. There is no gentle way to say this. James Braun has been found in his study. He is dead. The storm has the roads; no one is leaving, and no one from outside is getting in. Which means the person who did this is still in the house. They are standing among us right now — and until we find them, every one of us sleeps under the same roof as a killer.
study_scene: The study door swings open on a room gone wrong. The desk chair lies on its side. James Braun's crystal nightcap glass rests where it fell, a last ring of brandy at the bottom — smoked plum, and under it something bitter that doesn't belong in any bottle. The ledger drawer stands forced and empty. The desk lamp is cold. And look closely: the glass was poured from a bottle, and there is no bottle in this room. Someone brought it up. Someone poured it. And when it was done, someone carried it away.
house_rules: The rules of the house, and of the evening. One: you are your character tonight — their voice, their secrets, their grudges. Everything you need is on your phone. Two: you may lie, mislead, and perform anywhere in this house — except at trial. When you stand accused at trial and are asked a direct question, you must answer it truthfully as your character. Three: the roped areas are roped for a reason, and the real valuables are Mr. Braun's, not props — admire, don't handle. Four: when a trial is called, everyone comes. No exceptions, no alibis. Five: be suspicious, be dramatic, be somebody. The dead man would insist.
reveal_paragraphs: Here is how James Braun died. The bottle that appeared in his study — a 'peace offering' of Roka Reserve — began the evening in Solomon Roka's crates in the west extension. It passed through the kitchen, where Dr. Aiko Nishimoto, the family physician who had already visited the study once that night, added a tincture of her own preparation: bitter, botanical, and certain. Then Carla Lucciano signed out the study passkey at 9:33, and when Sutton Brady seized the stage at 9:40 and brought the champagne tower down, the halls emptied — and Carla walked the side path, in through the service door, and set the bottle on the desk of a man who trusted his own front gate more than his own staff.

Three hands, one murder. Solomon Roka supplied the signature — his own label, the one bottle missing from crate RR-11, the smoked plum anyone could smell in the corridor. Dr. Nishimoto supplied the means — the poison, drawn from the same knowledge that answered a banker's innocent letters about medicinal plants until the questions got too close. And Carla Lucciano supplied the access — the keys, the raked path, the fifteen minutes nobody watches a driveway. Behind them stood the Syndicate's associates: Giuliana Andolpho, who left the calling card that made Braun open his door to a gift, and Sutton Brady, who made two hundred people look the other way at exactly 9:41.

And the why is in the drawer they emptied. James Braun had spent a year building a ledger on the Midnight Syndicate — its routes, its fronts, its friends in fine rooms — and at midnight tonight he was going to hand it to Detective Remington Whitley and buy himself a clean exit from a dirty decade. The Syndicate does not permit exits. Not his, and not the ledger's. So spare a thought for the ones who only looked guilty: Wilhelm Shepard, sweating over bribes, not blood. Priya Patel, carrying her father's name like a sentence. Da'Quan Wilson, whose loudest crime was a marketing campaign. The snails were everywhere tonight. Only three of them had shells worth breaking.
town_win: The gavel falls, and it falls true. Doctor, bootlegger, and chauffeur — all three of the Syndicate's hands, convicted under the roof they thought would hide them. The storm breaks toward morning, the roads open, and the cars that leave Braun Manor carry the guilty to jail and the innocent home to bed. The ledger is gone, but its author is answered for — and somewhere in the county, the Midnight Syndicate learns that a room full of frightened dinner guests did what courts and cops could not. Raise a glass. Check it first. But raise it. The house wins.
killer_win: The gavel falls, and it falls wrong. When the storm lifts and the driveway clears, at least one of the Syndicate's hands walks out of Braun Manor into the grey morning — free. Perhaps the doctor drives home and opens her patient list. Perhaps the bootlegger's trucks roll at dawn, one crate lighter. Perhaps the chauffeur simply takes her seat behind the wheel, gloves on, and waits for the next instruction. The ledger is ash, the witness is buried, and the snail draws its slow silver line onward through the county. You dined with them. You voted. And the Syndicate thanks you for your hospitality.
tamper_scrubbed: This scene has been disturbed — someone got here first.
